subject: system-design
title: Design WhatsApp
summary: Deliver 1:1 and group messages in real time, instantly online and reliably offline. It is built on persistent connections, a message router, and store-and-forward delivery.

blocks.text: A chat system has to feel instant when both people are online and stay reliable when one isn't. The core job is routing a message from a sender's phone to a recipient's phone in real time, and holding it safely when the recipient is offline. Everything else (receipts, presence, groups, media) hangs off that routing core.

items: Functional: send and receive 1:1 and group messages, with media (images, voice).
Delivery and read receipts (sent, delivered, read) and online presence.
Offline delivery: a message reaches its recipient even if they were offline when it was sent.
Low latency for online users; ordered, exactly-once-feeling delivery.

blocks.text: Billions of users and tens of billions of messages a day, with hundreds of millions of connections open at once. Messages are tiny, so the dominant cost isn't storage. It's holding a vast number of long-lived connections and fanning messages out with low latency. Media is offloaded so the message path stays light.

Each client holds a persistent WebSocket connection to a chat server, kept open so the server can push messages down at any moment. A message-routing service maps each user to the server holding their live connection, so it knows where to deliver.

items: Chat servers terminate WebSocket connections and push messages to connected clients.
A presence/session registry maps user → which chat server holds their connection.
The routing service finds the recipient's connection and delivers, or queues if they're offline.
Media (images, voice notes) uploads to a blob store; only a reference travels through the message path.
A message store persists in-flight messages until delivery is confirmed.

blocks.title: Store-and-forward
blocks.text: When the recipient is offline, the message can't be pushed, so the server stores it in a per-user queue and forwards it on reconnect. Many designs delete the message once delivery is acknowledged. The server is a relay, not the long-term archive, which keeps storage small and aligns with end-to-end encryption.

A group message is fanned out: the server resolves the group's membership and routes a copy to each member, pushing to those online and queuing for those offline. Presence is tracked via the connection itself plus periodic heartbeats. When a socket drops or heartbeats stop, the user is marked offline, and status changes are pushed only to interested contacts to avoid a fan-out storm.

Messages are encrypted on the sender's device and decrypted only on the recipient's, so the server routes ciphertext it can't read. This shapes the design: the server can't index or search message content, encryption keys are exchanged between devices, and the message store holds only opaque blobs.

blocks.title: Receipts ride the same path
blocks.text: Delivery and read receipts are just small messages flowing back the other way. When a client receives or opens a message, it sends an ack the server routes to the original sender. Reuse the routing core rather than building a separate channel.
